body:
Found while writing the PMAT-251 dependency-update acceptance check; measured on `main` (`a359431e8f`, v7.0.3) and on the upgraded branch identically, so it is not a dependency effect.

## Reproducer

```
$ cargo build --workspace --all-targets
error: the crate `base64` requires panic strategy `abort` which is incompatible with this crate's strategy of `unwind`
error: could not compile `bashrs-wasm` (test "probar_shell_safety") due to 107 previous errors
```

```
$ cargo build -p bashrs-wasm --tests      # alone: fine
    Finished `dev` profile
```

## Cause (measured)

The root `Cargo.toml` sets `panic = "abort"` for `[profile.dev]`. When the whole workspace is built in one invocation, `base64` (a transitive dev-dependency of `bashrs-wasm` through `jugar-probar 1.0.4`) is unified into one unit compiled with `abort`, while the `probar_shell_safety` test harness needs `unwind`. Built alone, cargo compiles a separate `unwind` copy and the target links.

## Why it matters

CI runs `cargo test --workspace --lib` (nextest), so this never shows up there; anything that builds all targets in one go — `make`, a local `cargo build --workspace --all-targets`, an acceptance script — fails on a target CI never exercises. #233 (clippy scope) will hit the same wall when `--all-targets` is added.

## Options

1. Drop `panic = "abort"` from `[profile.dev]` (keep it in `release`/`dist`), or
2. move `probar_shell_safety` behind a feature that is off by default, or
3. document that `bashrs-wasm` test targets must be built with `-p bashrs-wasm`.
title: build: cargo build --workspace --all-targets fails on bashrs-wasm's probar test target (panic strategy abort vs unwind) — pre-existing, hidden by --lib in CI

body:
Found by the PMAT-251 corpus-growth lanes (entry `bash-idioms-adversarial-quotes-metacharacters`, kept out of the corpus as `docs/audits/corpus-pending-PMAT-251.jsonl`).

## Reproducer

```rust
fn main() { let s = "a `b` c"; println!("{}", s); }
```

```
$ bashrs build probe-backtick.rs
error[internal]: Validation error: Backtick command substitution detected in string literal (SC2006): 'a `b` c'
```

## Why this looks like a false rejection

The transpiler emits string literals single-quoted (`s='a `b` c'`), and inside single quotes a backtick is inert in every POSIX shell — there is no command substitution to detect. The validator rejects the Rust literal by content, before emission, so a program that merely *prints* a backtick (documentation strings, Markdown, regexes) cannot be transpiled at all. The same pre-emission check should be reviewed for `$(`, `$VAR` and `\` inside literals: the emitter's quoting is what decides whether they are live, not the literal's bytes.

## Expected

Either emit the literal single-quoted and accept it, or document the rejected byte set in the DSL reference and the `check` command's output so corpus generators can avoid it.

Measured on `bashrs 7.0.3`.
title: transpiler: a string literal containing a backtick is rejected before emission although the single-quoted output is inert

body:
Found by the PMAT-251 corpus-growth lane while checking the DSL surface (bashrs 7.0.3).

## Reproducer

```rust
fn main() { let items = ["a", "b"]; let joined = array_join(items, ","); println!("{}", joined); }
```

```
$ bashrs build probe-join.rs -o probe-join.sh && sh probe-join.sh
probe-join.sh: 40: items: parameter not set
```

## What is emitted

```sh
items_0='a'
items_1='b'
joined="$(rash_array_join "$items" ',')"
rash_println "$joined"
```

The array literal is lowered to `items_0`, `items_1`, but the stdlib call receives `"$items"`, which is never assigned. Under the generated `set -euf` the script aborts. `array_len(items)` and `for x in items` should be checked for the same lowering gap.

## Expected

`rash_array_join` receives the elements (newline-joined, which is what the runtime helper reads), e.g. `joined="$(printf '%s\n' "$items_0" "$items_1" | rash_array_join - ',')"` or an equivalent that the runtime helper already understands.

Measured on `bashrs 7.0.3` (crates.io install).
title: transpiler: array_join over a local array literal emits "$items" (unset) — script aborts under set -u

body:
`bashrs` honours its own native rule codes (`DET*`, `SEC*`, `IDEM*`, `REL*`) inside a **`# shellcheck disable=`** directive. shellcheck cannot parse that directive, and on failing to parse it **stops checking the file**. So the suppression works in bashrs and silently disables shellcheck for the whole file.

## Demonstration

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# shellcheck disable=DET002
v="a b"
ls $v
rm $v
```

**bashrs — the directive is honoured:**

```
$ bashrs lint sup.sh | grep -c DET002
0          # 3 without the directive
```

**shellcheck — the file is abandoned:**

```
$ shellcheck abort.sh
^-- SC1073 (error): Couldn't parse this shellcheck directive. Fix to allow more checks.
                        ^-- SC1072 (error): Expected '=' after directive key. ...
```

Nothing else is reported. With the directive line removed, the same file yields the two real findings that were being hidden:

```
$ shellcheck abort2.sh
   ^-- SC2086 (info): Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting.
   ^-- SC2086 (info): Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting.
```

`# shellcheck disable=SC2086` — a real shellcheck code — parses fine, so the trigger is specifically a non-`SC` code inside the shellcheck namespace.

## Why this is bashrs's to fix

`DET002` is a bashrs rule. bashrs is the only tool that gives that string meaning, and by accepting it in shellcheck's directive namespace it makes writing the broken form the path of least resistance: the user sees a DET002 error, reaches for the suppression comment shape they already know, confirms bashrs goes quiet, and never learns that shellcheck stopped running.

Measured in `paiml/paiml-mcp-agent-toolkit`, where bashrs and shellcheck both run: `scripts/record-metric.sh`, `scripts/validate-metrics.sh` and `scripts/implement-dependency-reduction.sh` each carry `# shellcheck disable=DET002` and are therefore **entirely unchecked by shellcheck** — three files, discovered only by running both tools and diffing. One of them (`validate-metrics.sh`) also carries the correct `# bashrs disable-file=DET002` on the next line, so the shellcheck-namespaced copy is pure loss.

## Expected

`# shellcheck disable=` should be honoured only for `SC`-numbered codes. A bashrs-native code appearing there should be reported — something like *"DET002 is a bashrs rule; use `# bashrs disable-file=DET002`. A non-SC code in a `# shellcheck` directive makes shellcheck abandon the file."* That converts a silent loss of coverage into a one-line fix.

## Secondary, same subject: `disable-line` placement diverges from shellcheck

shellcheck's `# shellcheck disable=SC2086` on the line **above** applies to the following line. bashrs's `disable-line` only works on the **same** line:

| placement | DET002 suppressed |
|---|---|
| `echo "$(date)" > VERSION # bashrs disable-line=DET002` | yes |
| `# bashrs disable-line=DET002` on the preceding line | **no — silently ignored** |
| `# bashrs disable-file=DET002` on the preceding line | yes |

DET002's own message says *"suppress with `# bashrs disable-line=DET002`"* without saying where to put it, and the preceding-line placement is the one shellcheck users will reach for first. It fails silently, which is the same failure mode as #240.

## Environment

- bashrs 6.67.0
- shellcheck 0.8.0
- Related: #240 (closed) — silently ignored suppression directives.
title: bashrs honours its native codes in `# shellcheck disable=`, which makes shellcheck abort the whole file — suppression works in one tool and silently disables the other

body:
## Summary

On identical files, `bashrs lint` emits `SC2046` **210 times** where shellcheck 0.8.0 emits **1**, and `SC2086` **97 times** where shellcheck emits **12**. Since bashrs reuses shellcheck's `SC` numbering, users reasonably expect comparable semantics; at a 200:1 ratio the code cannot be triaged.

## Method

Both linters run over the same 40 tracked `*.sh` files in `paiml/paiml-mcp-agent-toolkit`, counted by rule code. `bashrs 6.67.0`, `shellcheck 0.8.0`.

```
code       bashrs  shellcheck
SC2046        210           1
SC2086         97          12
SC1004         75           0
SC1078         40           0
SC2183         27           0
SC2047         23           0
SC1009         21           0
SC2164         21           0
SC1028         19           0
SC2161         18           0
SC2036         10           0
SC2101         10           0
SC2154         10           0
```

Every file in the sample passes `bash -n`.

## Known contributors

Some of the `SC2046` volume is the arithmetic-expansion mis-tokenisation filed separately (`$(( ))` parsed as `$( )`, which yields a spurious `SC2046` per occurrence). That will not account for all of it.

## Two codes appear to carry non-shellcheck meanings

Worth confirming these are intentional, because reusing an `SC` number for a different rule makes cross-tool triage misleading:

- **SC2047** — bashrs emits *"Quote $n to prevent word splitting, or use [[..]] instead of [..]"*. On the same line shellcheck emits **SC2086** for the same underlying issue. Correct finding, and it looks like the wrong number.
- **SC2183** — bashrs emits *"Variable used as command name - potential injection risk"*, e.g. on `$sh_c 'docker version'` where `sh_c` holds `sh -c`. shellcheck reports nothing there.

## Ask

Either align the `SC*` codes with shellcheck's semantics, or move bashrs-specific rules into the bashrs-native namespace (as `SEC*` / `DET*` / `REL*` / `IDEM*` already are), so an `SC` number means one thing across tools.
title: SC2046 fires 210x and SC2086 8x more than shellcheck on identical files; SC2047/SC2183 carry non-shellcheck meanings

body:
Running the full `dogfood` pre-release protocol against v6.67.0 for the first time surfaced two structural, pre-existing, repo-wide quality gaps. Both were verified as pre-existing (not introduced by the v6.67.0 release work) before filing. Neither blocks the v6.67.0 release: nothing in CI currently gates on either.

## 1. CB-200 TDG Grade Gate: 120 functions below grade A, 107 files at F

```
$ pmat comply check
✗ CB-200: TDG Grade Gate: 120 function(s) below minimum grade A
```

Sample (full list of ~120 in the CI job log / attached below):

```
rash/src/corpus/expansion_generator.rs:309 generate_makefile_templates [B] (complexity: 12)
rash/src/corpus/evaluation.rs:42 evaluate [B] (complexity: 14)
rash/src/corpus/runner.rs:112 run_entry_with_trace [B] (complexity: 13)
rash/src/corpus/oip.rs:47 fmt [B] (complexity: 17)
rash/src/make_parser/parser_parse.rs:240 parse_target_rule [B] (complexity: 13)
rash/src/make_parser/purify/reproducible_builds.rs:9 analyze_reproducible_builds [B] (complexity: 14)
rash/src/validation/pipeline_string_validators.rs:166 validate_expr_in_exec_context [B] (complexity: 17)
rash/src/validation/pipeline.rs:190 validate_ir_recursive [B] (complexity: 16)
```

107 files score an outright F grade, capping the whole-project TDG score at B regardless of the other ~930 files, e.g.:

```
./rash/src/config/aliaser.rs (25.2)
./rash/src/config/nondeterminism.rs (41.9)
./rash/src/config/quoter.rs (25.2)
./rash/src/formatter/dialect.rs (0.1)
./rash/src/linter/make_preprocess.rs (41.9)
./rash/src/linter/rules/perf001.rs (15.1)
./rash/src/linter/rules/perf003.rs (15.1)
./rash/src/linter/rules/perf005.rs (25.2)
./rash/src/linter/rules/sc1026.rs (25.2)
./rash/src/linter/rules/sc1036.rs (41.9)
... and 97 more
```

**Verified pre-existing**, not introduced by v6.67.0: sampled 8 of the F-grade files (`aliaser.rs`, `nondeterminism.rs`, `quoter.rs`, `dialect.rs`, `make_preprocess.rs`, `perf001.rs`, `sc1026.rs`, `sc1036.rs`) — each one's last modification predates `v6.66.3` by multiple releases. This is accumulated complexity debt spanning the codebase's history, not something from the six-ticket lint-fix release.

**Why it has never gated a release**: nothing in `.github/workflows/` runs `pmat comply check` or any TDG-grade check. It was only surfaced by running the (new-to-this-repo) `dogfood` pre-release protocol, which treats CB-200 as a hard gate — see paiml/bashrs#233 for the related finding that CI's clippy also only ever checks the `bashrs-specs` workspace-root stub, not `rash/`, so a comparable gap exists on the clippy side.

## 2. `pv lint contracts/` — 89 errors, all in a sibling repository

```
$ pv lint contracts/
Summary: 89 errors, 11 warnings, 0 suppressed
Result: FAIL
```

Every one of the 89 errors is the identical schema mismatch:

```
[ERROR] PV-VAL-001 — YAML parse error: Failed to parse YAML: verification_summary: missing field `total_obligations` at line 5 column 3
```

`contracts/` in this repo is almost entirely **symlinks** into `../provable-contracts/contracts/` (a separate repository, `paiml/provable-contracts`, with its own remote and release cadence):

```
$ ls -la contracts/
encoder-roundtrip-v1.yaml -> ../provable-contracts/contracts/encoder-roundtrip-v1.yaml
linter-coverage-v1.yaml -> ../provable-contracts/contracts/linter-coverage-v1.yaml
... (9 of 10 files are symlinks)
```

The one file that lives in *this* repo, `contracts/linter-logical-lines-v1.yaml`, passes `pv lint` cleanly (0 errors). So this is `pv` 0.49.0 requiring a `verification_summary.total_obligations` field that predates the contracts in `provable-contracts` — **not fixable by a bashrs commit**; the fix belongs in `paiml/provable-contracts`, either by regenerating those 9 contracts' `verification_summary` blocks or by `pv` treating the field as optional/defaulted for older contracts.

## Recommendation

- Track CB-200 here; work through the ~120 functions in batches the way the SEC010/SEC002/DET002 rewrites in v6.67.0 did — small, verified, one rule/module at a time — rather than a single mass refactor.
- File the `verification_summary.total_obligations` gap against `paiml/provable-contracts` (or `pv` itself if the field should be optional for schema versions before it was added).
- Consider adding `pmat comply check` (gating on CB-200 only, per the "unmeasured is not a pass" reasoning in the sovereign dogfood protocol) to CI once the backlog is cleared, so it cannot silently reaccumulate.
title: CB-200 TDG grade gate: 120 functions below grade A (107 F-grade files), pre-existing

body:
CI's `lint` job checks **one 5-test stub crate** and never looks at `rash/`, where essentially all of this project's code lives. Separately, **37 of the 145 integration test targets do not compile**, and nothing in CI builds them.

Both are measured below on `main` @ `4d54fb9d49` (v6.67.0), and both are pre-existing — the second is byte-identical at `v6.66.3`.

## 1. `ci / lint` lints the wrong package

The workspace root is *both* `[workspace]` and `[package] name = "bashrs-specs"`, and there is no `default-members`. So a bare `cargo clippy` resolves to the root package only:

```
$ cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings -A unused-variables   # exactly what CI runs
$ ... | grep -oE "Checking bashrs[a-z-]* v[0-9.]+" | sort -u
Checking bashrs-specs v6.67.0
```

That is the whole list. `rash/`, `bashrs-oracle/`, `bashrs-runtime/` and `bashrs-wasm/` are never linted by the gate.

This is the **same class of bug as GH-214**, which was fixed for *tests* by setting `test_workspace: true` in `ci.yml` — with a comment about "a rotting workspace member". The reusable workflow exposes `clippy_args` (default `--all-targets`); the identical hole was left open for clippy.

### What is actually behind it

Nothing in any library, which is why this is safe to close properly rather than urgently:

```
$ for m in bashrs bashrs-oracle bashrs-runtime bashrs-wasm bashrs-specs; do
      cargo clippy -p $m --lib -- -D warnings; done
  bashrs           PASS
  bashrs-oracle    PASS
  bashrs-runtime   PASS
  bashrs-wasm      PASS
  bashrs-specs     PASS
```

By target kind, workspace-wide:

| scope | errors |
|---|---|
| `--workspace --lib` | **0** |
| `--workspace --bins` | **0** |
| `--workspace --examples` | 2 |
| `--workspace --tests` | 178 |
| `--workspace --benches` | 212 |

The two example errors are one real lint (`literal with an empty format string` in `examples/shellsafetybench`). The `--tests` and `--benches` numbers are dominated by item 2.

## 2. 37 of 145 integration test targets do not compile

```
$ cargo build --workspace --tests --keep-going
$ ... | grep 'could not compile .* (test "' | sort -u | wc -l
37
$ ls rash/tests/*.rs | wc -l
145
```

Error kinds: `E0425` (cannot find function/value — 170), `E0282` (type annotations needed — 72), `E0433` (unresolved module — 41). The shape is the familiar orphan-extracted-fragment pattern: a file split out of a larger test module without its `use` statements, e.g. `NamedTempFile::new()` with no `use tempfile::NamedTempFile;`, and bare `predicate::` in 9+ files.

The 37:

```
canonical_matrix_test_matrix_prope        cli_comply_tests_tests_comply_cli
cli_dockerfile_purify_tests_dockerfile    cli_dockerfile_purify_tests_dockerfile_2
cli_error_handling_tests_main             cli_integration_tests_CLI
cli_integration_tests_CLI_2               cli_make_tests_tests_CLI
cli_property_tests                        cli_purify_tests_tests_PURIFY
cli_ssc_tests_tests_kaizen107_cl          cli_ssc_tests_tests_pmat142_corp
cli_ssc_tests_tests_ssb002_conve          cli_test_generate_tests
corpus_tests_tests_CORPUS_2               dockerfile_dcode_tests_tests_d020_numeric
falsification_probar_testing_tests_falsification
integration_tests                         integration_tests_main
integration_tests_main_part2 … part8      linter_bug_hunting_hunt
linter_tui_bug_hunting_hunt               linter_tui_bug_hunting_tests_hunt_frame
parser_bug_hunting_tests_control_flow     parser_probar_testing_tests_parser
simulation_probar_testing_simulation_e    test_fix_safety_taxonomy_tests_property
transpiler_tcode_tests_tests_t022_groupin transpiler_tcode_tests_tests_t057_multipl
transpiler_tcode_tests_tests_t091_file    transpiler_tcode_tests_tests_t118_vec
```

**Pre-existing, and exactly so:** building the same targets at `v6.66.3` in a clean worktree gives the same **37**, the same set (one target-name spelling differs).

## Why it matters

- The release checklist in `CLAUDE.md` says "**Integration tests pass**: All CLI and end-to-end tests". That line is currently unverifiable — `cargo test -p bashrs --tests` cannot link. We have been ticking a box nobody can check.
- It blocks mutation testing entirely: `cargo mutants` aborts with *"cargo build failed in an unmutated tree"*, so the documented ≥90% mutation gate cannot run for anyone.
- Names like `cli_integration_tests_CLI`, `cli_purify_tests_tests_PURIFY` and `falsification_probar_testing` suggest real coverage of the CLI surface is dark.

## Suggested order

1. **Fix the 37 targets** (mostly adding `use` statements), or delete the ones that are dead fragments of an already-migrated module. Do this first — it is the prerequisite for step 2 being green.
2. **Then** set `clippy_args: --workspace --all-targets` in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, mirroring what `test_workspace: true` already does for tests, and fix the one real example lint.
3. Add `default-members` to the root `Cargo.toml`, or move `bashrs-specs` out of the root, so a bare `cargo <anything>` at the root stops silently meaning "the stub crate". That is the root cause of both GH-214 and this.
4. Once the tests link, wire `cargo test --workspace --tests` into CI so the release checklist line becomes true.

Do **not** do step 2 before step 1 — it turns the pipeline red immediately, which is how a gate teaches people to bypass it.
title: CI lints only the bashrs-specs stub, and 37 of 145 integration test targets do not compile

body:
Split out of #230, which landed in v6.67.0.

## What changed in 6.67.0

DET002 now fires only when a timestamp reaches a *reproducible sink* — an artifact name or contents, a hash input, a build id, a truncating redirect. That is the right contract for a **reproducibility** rule, and it is what #230 asked for.

One consequence: a timestamp that is only ever **compared** is no longer reported.

```sh
if [ "$(date +%s)" -gt 1700000000 ]; then
    echo "licence expired" >&2
    exit 1
fi
```

Nothing here reaches an artifact, so DET002 is correct to stay silent. An existing assertion (`test_DET002_still_flags_timestamp_in_logic`) expected a finding; it was renamed to `test_GH230_det002_comparison_sink_not_flagged` and inverted, because it encoded the old text-matching behaviour.

## Why this deserves a rule of its own

The concern behind that old assertion is real, but it is **not** reproducibility — it is **time-dependent control flow**. A script that branches on the wall clock:

- behaves differently depending on *when* it runs, so it is not testable by replay;
- is a classic source of "works on my machine, fails at 00:00 UTC" and of tests that pass for eleven months;
- can silently change a build's *output* without any timestamp appearing in that output.

Filing it as DET002 mislabels it: the message would talk about reproducible builds while the defect is a scheduling hazard, and the remedy (`SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`) does not apply.

## Proposal — DET005: time-dependent control flow

Fire when a wall-clock value reaches a **branch condition** rather than an artifact:

```sh
if [ "$(date +%H)" -lt 6 ]; then ... fi          # DET005
while [ "$(date +%s)" -lt "$deadline" ]; do ... done   # DET005
case "$(date +%u)" in 6|7) ... ;; esac           # DET005
[ "$(date +%s)" -gt "$expiry" ] && exit 1        # DET005
```

Do **not** fire on:

- a duration — `end=$(date +%s); elapsed=$(( end - start ))` and the `bc` form. Measuring elapsed time is the point of measuring elapsed time.
- a timeout loop with a bounded body where the comparison is against a *relative* deadline computed in the same script. (Debatable — decide explicitly and document it either way.)
- anything already reported by DET002, so the two rules do not double-report the same line.

Suggested severity: **Warning**, not Error. Unlike a timestamp in an artifact name, this is often deliberate (cron-style scripts, backoff loops), and #227/#230's whole lesson is that an unactionable `Error` gets the rule disabled rather than the code fixed.

## Where the machinery already is

`linter::timestamp_flow` (added in v6.67.0) already classifies sinks and has `is_test_context` / `condition_part`, which identify exactly the case DET005 wants — it currently uses them to classify the value as *benign*. DET005 would consume the same classification with the opposite polarity, so this is mostly a new rule module plus a `SinkClass::Conditional` variant, not new analysis.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] the four `DET005` examples above are reported at `warning`
- [ ] the duration examples are not reported by DET005 or DET002
- [ ] a line reported by DET002 is not also reported by DET005
- [ ] `book/src/linting/determinism.md` documents the split, so a reader who expected DET002 to catch this can find where it went
title: DET005: time-dependent control flow deserves its own rule, split from DET002
